name: Learn: Resource Quotas & Limit Ranges
objective: CKAD › Application Environment, Configuration and Security (25%). Goal: govern a namespace's resources — ResourceQuota (compute totals + object counts) and LimitRange (default and min/max per container) — and see how a quota forces pods to declare resources.
description: Namespace-level resource governance: cap total compute and object counts with ResourceQuota, and set per-container defaults and bounds with LimitRange.

questions.title: ResourceQuota — cap total compute
questions.teach:
A **ResourceQuota** caps the resources a namespace may consume. A *compute* quota tracks `requests.cpu`, `requests.memory`, `limits.cpu`, `limits.memory`. Create it with `kubectl create quota <name> --hard=... -n <ns>`.

**Gotcha:** once a compute quota exists, **every pod must declare the matching requests/limits** or it's rejected.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `quota-compute`, create a ResourceQuota named `compute-quota` with hard limits: `requests.cpu=1`, `requests.memory=1Gi`, `limits.cpu=2`, `limits.memory=2Gi`.

Target: `kubectl get resourcequota compute-quota -n quota-compute` shows those hard values.

verification.description: compute-quota has the four compute hard limits

questions.title: A pod that fits under the quota
questions.teach:
Because the compute quota exists, a pod with **no** resources is rejected. Give the container a `resources:` block with `requests` and `limits` that fit under the quota.

**Gotcha:** every dimension the quota tracks must be present — omit one `limits.*` value and admission still rejects the pod.
questions.prompt:
In `quota-compute`, create a pod `app` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) with container `requests` cpu `200m` / memory `256Mi` and `limits` cpu `500m` / memory `512Mi`. It must be admitted and reach Running.

Target: pod `app` is Running and declares those requests.
questions.hint: `kubectl run app -n quota-compute --image=busybox:1.36 --requests='cpu=200m,memory=256Mi' --limits='cpu=500m,memory=512Mi' --command -- sleep 3600` (or write YAML with a resources block).
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: quota-compute
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    resources:
      requests: {cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi}
      limits: {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi}
EOF

verification.description: pod 'app' is Running with resource requests set

questions.title: ResourceQuota — cap object counts
questions.teach:
A ResourceQuota can also cap the **number of objects** in a namespace. Use a built-in count name like `pods`, `services`, or `configmaps`: `--hard=pods=2` means at most two pods may exist at once.

**Gotcha:** counts are **current live objects**, not a cumulative total — delete a pod and the slot frees up again.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `quota-count`, create a ResourceQuota named `pod-quota` that limits the namespace to at most `2` pods.

Target: `pod-quota` has hard `pods: 2`.

questions.title: LimitRange — default requests & limits
questions.teach:
A **LimitRange** (type `Container`) injects resources into pods that omit them: `defaultRequest` supplies the **requests** and `default` the **limits**. A pod with no `resources:` block gets these automatically. **Gotcha:** defaults are injected at admission — verify on the pod with `kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'`, not from the YAML.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `lr-defaults`, create a LimitRange `defaults` (type `Container`) with `defaultRequest` cpu `200m` / memory `128Mi` and `default` (limits) cpu `500m` / memory `256Mi`. Then create a pod `nodefaults` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) with **no** resources block.

Target: pod `nodefaults`'s container ends up with the defaulted requests (`cpu=200m`) and limits (`cpu=500m`).
questions.hint: Apply the LimitRange YAML (type: Container, default + defaultRequest), then `kubectl run nodefaults -n lr-defaults --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600`; check with `kubectl get pod nodefaults -n lr-defaults -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: defaults
  namespace: lr-defaults
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 200m
      memory: 128Mi
    default:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 256Mi
EOF
kubectl run nodefaults -n lr-defaults --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600

verification.description: nodefaults got defaulted requests/limits from the LimitRange

questions.title: LimitRange — min and max bounds
questions.teach:
A LimitRange (type `Container`) can also enforce **min** and **max** bounds per container: `min` is the floor for requests, `max` the ceiling for limits. A container outside the range is rejected at admission.

**Gotcha:** in YAML a bare integer like `cpu: 1` should be quoted (`cpu: "1"`) to keep it a string and avoid surprises.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `lr-minmax`, create a LimitRange `constraints` (type `Container`) with `min` cpu `100m` and `max` cpu `1`.

Target: the LimitRange has `max.cpu=1` and `min.cpu=100m`.
questions.hint: Apply a LimitRange YAML with `type: Container`, `min: {cpu: 100m}`, `max: {cpu: "1"}`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: constraints
  namespace: lr-minmax
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    min:
      cpu: 100m
    max:
      cpu: "1"
EOF

verification.description: constraints LimitRange has min/max cpu bounds
